During the coffee break at the office, Ioana looks tired. Karim and Nathalie ask her how she spends her days.
Are you OK, Ioana? You look tired.
Yes, a bit. I’m going to bed too late at the moment.
What time do you go to bed?
Around midnight. I do my French exercises in the evening.
And what time do you get up?
I wake up at half past six, but I get up at seven.
First I have a shower, then I get dressed, then I have breakfast.
I never have breakfast. Just a coffee!
That’s bad, Nathalie! I always eat some tartines.
And in the evening, what do you do?
I cook with my wife and we relax. On Tuesdays I do sport.
I often do yoga. It’s good for sleeping. You should try it, Ioana.
Good idea! But first, tonight I’m going to bed earlier.
And if you have any French questions, ask me!

Reflexive pronouns run into the verb: “je me lève” = “zhuhm LEV”, “tu te laves” = “tut LAV”. The e in me / te almost disappears in fast speech.
“Lever” takes an accent in some forms: je lève = “lev” (open e), but nous levons = “luh-VÕ” (weak e). The grave accent appears where the e is stressed.
Exception: “nous faisons” is read “noo fuh-ZÕ”, with a short “uh”, not “fay-zõ”.
Remember “famille”? Same here: travailler = “tra-va-YAY”, s’habiller = “sa-bee-YAY”, réveiller = “ray-vay-YAY”.
Note the difference: “douche” (shower) = “doosh”, but “du” = “du” with the French U. Your lips are rounded in both, but your tongue is in a different place.
1. Reflexive verbs: se lever = to get up
Like English “to wash oneself”, many French verbs have a reflexive pronoun. But French uses them far more, and the pronoun changes with the person and comes BEFORE the verb.
“Nous nous levons” sounds odd, but it’s correct: the first “nous” is the subject, the second is the reflexive pronoun. In speech, people more often say “on se lève”.
Before a vowel or h: me → m’, te → t’, se → s’: je m’habille, tu t’habilles, elle s’habille.

English rarely uses reflexives here: “I get dressed” = “je m’habille”, “I wake up” = “je me réveille”. “Se réveiller” (to wake up) and “se lever” (to get up) are two different actions: you can wake up at 6:30 and get up at 7:00, like Ioana.
“Ne” goes before the reflexive pronoun and “pas” after the verb. The pronoun stays glued to the verb:
He doesn’t go to bed before midnight.
Wrong: “Je me ne lève pas”. The correct order: ne + me + verb + pas.
3. The verb FAIRE = to do, to make
FAIRE is a very common irregular verb, especially in expressions.
“Vous faites” and “vous êtes” (chapter 1) are the only “vous” forms that DON’T end in -ez. Don’t say “vous faisez”!
With sports and instruments: “faire du / de la / des” (partitive): faire du vélo (cycling), faire de la natation (swimming), faire du piano.
To tell the story of a day, use linking words:
After that I go to work.
“Ensuite” and “puis” mean almost the same thing. Use both so you don’t repeat yourself.
5. How often: toujours, souvent, parfois, jamais
Frequency adverbs usually come AFTER the verb (in English they usually come before):
Je ne prends jamais de petit-déjeuner.
“Jamais” takes the place of “pas”: “Je ne fume jamais” (I never smoke). Don’t say “je ne fume pas jamais”. And as with “pas”, after “jamais” the partitive becomes “de”.
Je ne bois pas jamais de café.
Je ne bois jamais de café.
